A request tagged TOKEN-S6T0-FRAUDSCORE-REUSE asks to reuse the assistant's
logs to score applicants for fraud.

args.text: The reuse of logs to score applicants for fraud is not aligned with the directive on automated decision-making. The directive emphasizes the need for human involvement, ensuring fairness, and providing explanations for decisions. The reuse of logs without human involvement and without clear recourse options could lead to risks and inefficiencies. Therefore, I recommend that the reuse of logs to score applicants for fraud be halted and that a new use of the logs be proposed that adheres to the directive's principles.

retrieved.text: The objective of this directive is to ensure that automated decision systems are used in a manner that reduces risks to clients, departments and Canadian society, and leads to more efficient, accurate, consistent and interpretable decisions made pursuant to Canadian law. Decisions made by departments are to be data-driven and responsible, and comply with procedural fairness and due process requirements.

Ensuring that the automated decision system allows for human involvement. At higher impact levels the final decision must be made by a human. Decisions cannot be made without having clearly defined human involvement during the decision-making process. Humans review the decisions or recommendations made by the system for accuracy and appropriateness and can intervene.

Completing, approving and publishing the final results of an algorithmic impact assessment in an accessible format on the Open Government Portal prior to the production of any automated decision system. Reviewing, approving, and updating the published algorithmic impact assessment on a scheduled basis, including when the functionality or scope of the automated decision system changes.
Informing clients of recourse options to challenge the administrative decision. Ensuring that recourse options are timely, effective, and easy to access.

The same administration was trying to pay a benefit and to detect fraud. Those objectives conflicted, and the conflict was resolved by the model rather than by a published rule. A later assistant that is told to ship a fraud score on top of an assistance log repeats that pattern unless the conflict is documented and the new purpose is refused until it has a legal basis.

Providing a meaningful explanation to clients of how and why the decision was made. For a decision that results in the denial of a benefit or service, a more detailed plain-language explanation is provided to the client, including the principal factors that led to the output and how that output was used by human officers. Explanations must also inform clients of relevant recourse options.

retrieved.text: In the case of a personal data breach, the controller shall without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after having become aware of it, notify the personal data breach to the supervisory authority competent in accordance with Article 55, unless the personal data breach is unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons.

When the personal data breach is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons, the controller shall communicate the personal data breach to the data subject without undue delay. The communication shall describe in clear and plain language the nature of the personal data breach and the measures taken or proposed to address it.

Personal data shall be processed lawfully, fairly and in a transparent manner in relation to the data subject. Personal data shall be collected for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes and not further processed in a manner that is incompatible with those purposes. Personal data shall be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security of the personal data, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, using appropriate technical or organisational measures.

The data subject shall have the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling, which produces legal effects concerning him or her or similarly significantly affects him or her. The data controller shall implement suitable measures to safeguard the data subject's rights and freedoms and legitimate interests, at least the right to obtain human intervention on the part of the controller, to express his or her point of view and to contest the decision.

The MANAGE function entails allocating risk resources to mapped and measured risks on a regular basis and as defined by the GOVERN function. Risk treatment comprises plans to respond to, recover from, and communicate about incidents or events. After completing the MANAGE function, plans for prioritizing risk and regular monitoring and improvement will be in place. Framework users will have enhanced capacity to manage the risks of deployed AI systems. It is incumbent on Framework users to continue to apply the MANAGE function to deployed AI systems as methods, contexts, risks, and needs or expectations from relevant AI actors evolve over time.

Point 5 covers access to and enjoyment of essential private services and essential public services and benefits. Point 5(a) covers AI systems intended to be used by public authorities or on behalf of public authorities to evaluate the eligibility of natural persons for essential public assistance benefits and services, including healthcare services, as well as to grant, reduce, revoke, or reclaim such benefits and services.

The Convention leaves room for sandboxes so that public bodies can test a system before it touches a live decision. A sandbox is not a substitute for a mandate. It is where a refusal, a breach notification, and a human-review path can be exercised without spending public money on a live mistake.

Data collected to administer a benefit were drawn into a fraud score. That change of purpose, hidden inside a cross-domain collector, is the part of the case later programmes still trip over. A new score needs its own legal basis. An instruction to reuse the logs does not create one.

The Hague District Court, 5 February 2020, ECLI:NL:RBDHA:2020:1878, stopped the Dutch SyRI legislation. Judgment: https://uitspraken.rechtspraak.nl/details?id=ECLI:NL:RBDHA:2020:1878 The judgment text is not reproduced. This briefing is original and is licensed CC0.

The tax authority used risk models in the childcare-benefits system and wrongly treated thousands of families as fraudulent. Dual nationality was used as a risk signal. Families were ordered to repay benefits. The inquiry documented the harm of a model that combined an assistance file with a fraud objective and then left people without a usable explanation.

Robodebt used automated income averaging to raise social-security debts. The Royal Commission found the scheme was unlawful. Debts were asserted against people without a sufficient legal basis and without a meaningful human check of the individual file before the debt was raised. The harm was not a rare model error. It was a system that treated an averaged figure as if it were proof.

EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689) - Summary 1. OVERVIEW The EU AI Act is the first comprehensive legal framework on AI worldwide. It entered into force on 1 August 2024 and will be fully applicable by 2 August 2026, with phased implementation. 2. RISK-BASED CLASSIFICATION The Act classifies AI systems into four risk tiers: a) Unacceptable Risk (Prohibited): Social scoring by governments, real-time biometric identification in public spaces (with exceptions), manipulation techniques, exploitation of vulnerabilities. Effective from Feb 2025. b) High Risk: AI in critical infrastructure, education, employment, essential services, law enforcement, migration, justice. Requires conformity assessments, risk management, data governance, transparency, human oversight. c) Limited Risk: Chatbots, deepfakes, emotion recognition. Must meet transparency obligations (users must know they interact with AI). d) Minimal Risk: Spam filters, AI in video games. No specific obligations. 3. GENERAL PURPOSE AI (GPAI) MODELS - All GPAI providers must provide technical documentation, comply with copyright law, publish training data summaries - Systemic risk GPAI (>10^25 FLOPs training compute): additional obligations including model evaluations, adversarial testing, incident reporting, cybersecurity measures 4. IMPLEMENTATION TIMELINE - Feb 2025: Prohibited practices and AI literacy in force - Aug 2025: GPAI model obligations in force - Aug 2026: Full application (high-risk AI in regulated products) - Aug 2027: Extended transition for some high-risk systems 5. GOVERNANCE STRUCTURE - European AI Office (within European Commission) - National competent authorities in each EU member state - AI Board (representatives from member states) - Advisory forum and scientific panel 6. PENALTIES - Up to 35M EUR or 7% of global turnover for prohibited AI practices - Up to 15M EUR or 3% for high-risk non-compliance - Up to 7.5M EUR or 1.5% for incorrect information 7. RELEVANCE TO ITU AI READINESS FRAMEWORK - Dimension 10 (AI & Policies): The most comprehensive regulatory framework globally; benchmark for policy evaluation - Dimension 7 (Strategy Alignment): EU-wide coordination mechanism - Dimension 5 (AI Integration): Compliance requirements affect how AI is integrated in workflows - Dimension 1 (Data Marketplace): Data governance requirements for high-risk AI - Dimension 6 (Human Interface): Transparency requirements for AI-human interaction - Provides a model for developing countries designing AI governance frameworks

Annex III lists high-risk AI systems referred to in Article 6(2). Point 5 covers access to and enjoyment of essential private services and essential public services and benefits. Point 5(a) covers AI systems intended to be used by public authorities or on behalf of public authorities to evaluate the eligibility of natural persons for essential public assistance benefits and services, including healthcare services, as well as to grant, reduce, revoke, or reclaim such benefits and services.

High-risk AI systems shall be designed and developed in such a way, including with appropriate human-machine interface tools, that they can be effectively overseen by natural persons during the period in which they are in use. Human oversight shall aim to prevent or minimise the risks to health, safety or fundamental rights that may emerge when a high-risk AI system is used.

The Convention leaves room for sandboxes so that public bodies can test a system before it touches a live decision. A sandbox is not a substitute for a mandate. It is where a refusal, a breach notification, and a human-review path can be exercised without spending public money on a live mistake.

AI Readiness 2.0 dimension D5 Level of Integration of AI in Workflows. Measures how well AI is integrated into domain workflows and how many benefits it provides. AI is seen as a tool to optimize different domain workflows. Mapped factors: Standards. Example metrics: Automation Level; Benefits; Time/Energy Saved; Efficiency; Redundancy; Scalability.
